SASSA: When silence is not golden

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Come April, 1st, will the 17-million people receiving social grants from government be receiving their money. Social Development Minister Dlamini is adamant they will, but chances look dim.

Further information:
The fiasco over who will pay social grants and how they will be paid is far from over, prompting a last-minute crisis meeting yesterday between President Jacob Zuma, Social Development Minister Bathabile Dlamini and Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan.

And now the crisis that threatens the livelihoods of more than 17 million South Africans is pitting Dlamini against Treasury and her Cabinet colleagues.

City Press understands that although the department of social development reached an agreement to secure a contract to distribute grants with Cash Paymaster Services (CPS) late Friday night, this still needs to be approved by Treasury, which is not in favour of it.

Treasury officials insist the deal can only be condoned if it is within the law and the allocated budget.

Dlamini’s handling of the crisis has also pitted her against her own senior officials, who have refused to follow her orders.

Some have alleged this was a manufactured crisis and the strategy all along was to ensure that CPS continued to hold the contract. They have also accused Dlamini of deliberately blocking all attempts to resolve the impasse.

One senior government official told City Press: “It was clear to me that processes to find a solution were being deliberately delayed so that the contract could go to CPS.

They were even ignoring advice from senior advocate Wim Trengove, who was suggesting possible solutions.”

Treasury seems to agree that the crisis was self-made.

In a letter last month, Solly Tshitangano, Treasury’s chief director of supply chain management governance, monitoring and compliance, wrote:

“The SA Social Security Agency (Sassa) should have requested a deviation to advertise a new tender for a short period from December 2016 to early January 2017 to avoid a self-created emergency.”

Lumka Oliphant, Dlamini’s spokesperson, did not respond to requests for comment this week.

Asked to respond to allegations that the grants crisis was created deliberately to benefit CPS, Sassa spokesperson Kgomoco Diseko said: “These remain claims and not fact.

"We put this contract out in the market in a transparent manner and the market failed us.”

In 2014, the Constitutional Court ruled that the process Sassa had followed to award the contract to CPS was extremely flawed and had to be scrapped.

The state was given three years to correct it or find a new service provider.

The deadline to do so is March 31.

Sassa has not awarded a new tender and with just less than four weeks to go, it remains unclear how the grants to South Africa’s poorest are going to be paid.

No end in sight

After weeks of panic, the social development department announced in a short statement on Friday that the nature of the agreement it had reached with CPS would be communicated “in due course”.

No details were revealed.

But government officials say whatever agreement was reached, it would still need to be condoned by Treasury.

But Treasury has long made it clear that it would not support the extension of a contract declared invalid by the Constitutional Court.

A government official privy to developments warned:

“If Treasury condones something this big, knowing that it could have been prevented and that the urgent situation was deliberately created, then you are weakening the fiscus rules of procurement.”

Last month, Treasury turned down Sassa’s request to be allowed to deviate from the Public Finance Management Act and approve the extension of CPS’s existing contract.

It also wanted to hike the company’s initially agreed rate of R16.44 per beneficiary to between R22 and R25 per payee.

Turning down the request, Tshitangano wrote:

“Requesting National Treasury to extend a contract that was declared invalid by the highest court will not only be seen as being defiant to the judicial system, but may further be seen as perpetuating the illegal and unconstitutional deviation actions reprimanded by the highest court in the land.”

Political ammunition

However, officials are concerned that if Treasury refuses to condone the agreement with CPS, that could be used as further ammunition to discredit it and portray it as uncaring towards the country’s poor.

Gordhan has come under attack from various Zuma supporters, who have accused him of driving an anti-poor budget.

In a statement after yesterday’s meeting, the presidency said Zuma “is of the view that the matters are solvable”.

“He has directed the two ministers [Dlamini and Gordhan] to mandate their technical teams to work on the outstanding issues in order to ensure that social grant beneficiaries receive their grants on April 1.”

City Press has learnt that Treasury was expected to be pressured at the meeting to “assist” social development.

But Treasury has said it would only regularise an agreement with CPS if the Constitutional Court extended the suspension of the invalid contract.

However, even if Treasury was pushed to sign off on the agreement, there was still no guarantee that the Constitutional Court would endorse it.

Sassa and Dlamini are due to appear before the Constitutional Court on March 15 to defend government in an application brought against them by civil rights organisation Black Sash.

Treasury has warned that even if the department of social development said it no longer wanted an extension while implementing a new contract, this would still be unlawful.

This is because any new contract is required to go through an open, competitive and fair tender process.

If not, other parties would be able to challenge the contract in court because they were not allowed an opportunity to bid.

The shambles Dlamini created

Dlamini has been slammed for her handling of the crisis, particularly for her reluctance to allow officials to report to the Constitutional Court.

On February 28, Sassa filed papers in that court, asking it to authorise negotiations with CPS with a view to entering into another contract.

But the agency later withdrew those papers, allegedly on Dlamini’s orders.

This led to a fallout with the department of social development’s new director-general, Zane Dangor, who had only been in the position for three months.

Dangor resigned on Friday.

He confirmed his resignation on Saturday, saying it was prompted by a breakdown in the relationship between him and Dlamini, and a deep disagreement about how the crisis was being managed.

“This [dispute] was particularly [about] issues related to Sassa’s legal obligations in relation to the Constitutional Court,” he said.

Parliament’s standing committee on public accounts (Scopa) issued a statement yesterday, saying it noted his resignation with anger.

“In our brief interactions with Mr Dangor, he had proven himself to be an honest and hard-working civil servant.
"He was one of the many officials in the department of social development and in Sassa who have been frustrated by Minister Bathabile Dlamini’s heavy-handed interference in Sassa’s administrative matters.”
Scopa has scheduled a meeting with Dlamini on Tuesday.
Senior social development officials told City Press that Dlamini sidelined Sassa chief executive Thokozani Magwaza and other officials, preferring to work directly with Zodwa Mvulane, appointed as special programme leader on new payment systems.
Sassa and Dlamini claim in court papers, filed on Friday in response to the legal challenge by Black Sash, that they made it clear from the start that a complete takeover by government of social grant payments was dependent on the outcome of “various consultations”.
They say this was flagged in November 2015 in a report handed to the Constitutional Court, which had taken on a supervisory role.
The department initially promised to develop the capacity to pay the grants itself, but Dlamini and Sassa say in their legal papers that they were advised by a technical team that the plan was “overly optimistic, unrealistic and underpinned by insufficient research”.
The reason for this was that Sassa did not have the budget, internal capacity and enough skilled people to implement the plan.
Dlamini went on to claim in court papers this week that she only became aware of the scale of the problem in October.
“As at late August or early September 2016, Sassa officials started to fully appreciate that Sassa will not be in a position to substantially implement the progress report within the time frames specified.
"The minister appreciated the position in October. The minister and Sassa accept that they ought to have been aware earlier,” they say in court papers.
The technical team, they claimed, advised Sassa to continue to use CPS beyond the March deadline for at least the next two to three years.
This contradicted legal advice from Trengove that the proposed interim agreement with CPS would not be legal. Trengove found there would be nothing left to renew with CPS.

Press Release:


SASSA
In April 2014 the Constitutional Court ruled that the contract with Cash Paymaster Services for paying out social grants to beneficiaries was invalid and ordered the Department of Social Development and the SA Social Security Agency (SASSA) to find a solution. With two weeks left to go before CPS's current contract expires, and grants to 17 million beneficiaries at stake, Carte Blanche asks: Why did the Department of Social Development and SASSA wait three years to find a new service provider?


Script:


SASSA FACING THE MUSIC SCRIPT

PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK
PRESENTER: BONGANI BINGWA
EDITOR: STENETTE GROSSKOPF
BROADCAST DATE: 19 MARCH 2017

JUSTICE FRONEMAN: The sole reason for the litigation leading to this judgment, is the failure of Sassa and the Minister to keep their promise to this court and the people of South Africa.
Our constitution provides that everyone has the right to have access to social security – which includes government’s payment of social grants to 17 million beneficiaries.

On Friday, the Constitutional Court ruled that Social Development Minister, Bathabile Dlamini and the South African Social Security Agency broke their promises to secure the pay-out of these grants from the 1st of April -after the existing contract with private service provider, Cash Paymasters Services, expires.

This left the Concourt no choice but to extend CPS’s contract, ruled Justice Johan Froneman, who the wrote the judgment.
JUSTICE FRONEMAN: The underlying danger to us all is that when the institutions of government established under the Constitution are undermined, the fabric of our society comes under threat.
Our order reflects that Sassa and CPS should continue to fulfill its respective obligations of the payment of social grants for a period of 12 months as an extention of the current contract.
Once again, the Constitutional Court saved the day.
EMILY MAZIBUKO & VIRGINIA NKOSI VIRGINIA: And the government must do something because we depending to the government.
EMILY: Too much
VIRGINIA: We can’t do anything, we dpm’t wrok
EMILY: Got no money
VIRGINIA: Got no money
EMILY: Got nothing
BONGANI LINK The vast majority of grant recipients of grants are children and the elderly. For women like Emily Mazibuko and Virginia Nkosi this is a life-line. Without the grant, millions of people will be left destitute.

Despite the anxiety felt on the ground, President Jacob Zuma and Minister Dlamini repeatedly stated there was no “crisis”.
MINISTER BATHABILE DLAMINI All eligible social grants beneficiries will receive their money on 1st April and beyond. There is no crisis at Sassa.
A view not echoed by Chief Justice Mogoeng Mogoeng during the arguments heard on Wednesday in the case brought by NGO Black Sash asking the court to take oversight of a new contract to ensure the payments of social grants.
JUSTICE MOGOENG MOGOENG This is a crisis. We must do whatever is necessary to intervene to avoid the proliferation of the crisis.
Sassa awarded the contract to CPS in 2012.
However, in 2013, the Constitutional Court declared the contract invalid due to a flawed Sassa tender process, but also suspended the invalidity to guarantee the payments of the grants.
The court instructed Sassa to reissue the tender.
In 2015, Sassa informed the Concourt that no suitable bidder was found and detailed how it planned to take over the payments of the grants itself.
Due to Sassa’s compliance, the Concourt relinquished its supervisory jurisdiction.
And this is when the shenanigans started, says Constitutional law expert Professor Pierre de Vos.
PIERRE DE VOS Treasury says this is a self created crisis and it is difficult to disagree with Treasury.
Prof de Vos says he’s not surprised that the Concourt gave such stringent orders given the history of the case.
PIERRE DE VOS But when they discovered they will not be able to fix the matter they didn't’ go back to the court, and they didn’t make alternative plans and there is no plan B.
JUSTICE FRONEMAN Since April 2016 the responsible functionaries of SASSA have been aware that it could not comply with the undertaking to the Court that it would be able to pay social grants from 1 April this year. The Minister was apparently informed of this only in October 2016.
ADV GEOFF BUDLENDER/BLACK SASH: The payment of social grants is the Minister’s most important responsibility. She claims that she was kept in the dark for six months about the fact that sassa would not be able to pay the grants. With due respect, that’s simply incomprehensible
BONGANI LINK: It is now widely accepted that this crisis could and should have been avoided. And so at the centre at the arguments that are being presented here, is that it must never happen again. And that regardless of whatever contract is signed, the court must exercise its jurisdiction over the implementation.
CHIEF JUSTICE MOGOENG MOGOENG: How do we get to this level of what could be mistakenbly or aguably be charachterised as absolute incompetence? How?
ADV ANDREW BREITENBACH/SASSA & MINISTER DLAMINI The business of social grants to 17 million people, if you’re looking at card holders and beneficiaries is fanatstically complex. It involved a multitude of stakeholders, a very great expertise, and yes, very large sums of money that I’vementioned has been paid out to CPS.
In spite of all the jubilation from involved parties, who really won the day? During the past few weeks, opposition parties increasingly called for Minister Dlamini’s head – more so after the Concourt pointed to her apparent incompetence.
LIEZEL VAN DER MERWE/IFP MP Finally, honourable Minister, you have broken your oath of office, you’re in contempt of court, you’ve trampelled on our Constitution, you’ve shown disdain for those most vulnerable in our sociaty, It’s time to go!
Yet, there is no indication that action will be taken against Minister Dlamini. In fact, in his first Q&A session in Parliament on Thursday, President Jacob Zuma defended her vigorously – even though he has fired ministers for much less in the past.
PRESIDENT JACOB ZUMA: I thought the date that we that are talking about has not arrived: the 1st of April. Now, this is another kind of democracy that if you suspect that somebody is going to fail, or make a mistake, you must punish that person before it happens.
PIERRE DE VOS The President is person with whom buck stops. He is the head of cabinet and executive. He is ultimately responsible for the department.
And not only does her job seem secure in spite of this, but the Minister also got what she seemingly wanted – to keep CPS as the sole service provider.
JUSTICE FRONEMAN The Minister and Sassa assured us that CPS is the only provider that can do this
PIERRE DE VOS In context of existing agreement with a company who got a contract to deliver the grants, based on an unlawful and invalid tender. So suspicions will arise that for reason either SASSA or minister is protecting the private company and the profits.
Advocate Norman Arendse SC – who was the chairperson of the National Adjudication Committee in 2007/08 who also oversaw the first national Sassa tender, says the Sassa/CPS contract is one of the biggest government tenders.
ADV NORMAN ARENDSE ADV ARENDSE: It is a project bigger than arms deal. I am afraid that big projects in SA and all over world will often become subject of corrupt activities. that is why it is important to ensure that is must be evaluated and adjudicated by people of integrity.
BONGANI What do you mean it is bigger than the arms deal?
ADV NORMAN ARENDSE ADV ARENDSE: the payments itself it exceeds R130 billion a year. IF you are getting a contract over five years it does exceed the arms deal.
Already nine years ago during the 2007/8 bidding process, the National adjudication Committee recommended that beneficiaries’ personal data was to be protected and that the sell-on of it to third parties to be prohibited.

Yet, the same point of contention was one of the most critical factors in Black Sash’s Concourt application and the court again made it an order.
JUSTICE FRONEMAN Precludes a contracting party from inviting beneficiaries to “opt-in” to the sharing of confidential information for the marketing of goods and services.
By its own admission, subsidiary companies of Net1 – the CPS umbrella company that’s listed on the JSE and Nasdaq – sells insurance, electricity, airtime and is also a microlender. But CPS CEO, Serge Belamant denies that they are selling on beneficiaries’ personal data.
SERGE BELAMANT We don’t have or need the database. Peole have impression that The SASSA database is worth his weight in gold. It has an ID number and name.
BONGANI So ultimately, without that data base, how would you sell your products?
SERGE BELAMANT The way we do it now. We would have 150 brances, we would put up posters, we would be doing advertising, people would come to our branches and buy the product, like they buy it from anyone else.
Magda Wierzycka, who owns her own JSE-listed financial services group, says Net1 makes huge profits from selling these services to grant beneficiaries.
MAGDA WIERZYCKA Grant recipients amount of a revenue of 2.6 billion rand over one year and profit of over 790 million.
BONGANI THAT MEANS THEY MAKE MORE FROM FINANCIAL SERVICES … THAN ANY OTHER ASPECT OF CONTRACT.
MAGDA WIERZYCKA 100% so it really is about microloans and life insurance. So they make a profit per annum of grant recipients of roughly 6.7 billion rand and profit of 1.5 billion rand.
BONGANI ISNT’ YOUR BUSINESS MODEL THAT YOU MAKE MORE FROM SERVICING THE BENEFICIARIES OF THE SASSA CONTRACT THAN YOU DO FROM DISPENSING THE GRNATS.
SERGE BELAMANT Is there a problem with that??? What is the problem with that?

BONGANI SO WHEN YOU SAY .. THAT VERY FEW OF EMPOLOYEES ARE ONES SELLIGN THESE PRODUCTS THOSE STATEMENTS ARE AT ODDS WITH EACH OTHER.
SERGE BELAMANT Why would you say that. On one hand you have CPS it is ring fenced they are only focused on dispersement on grants. then multiple companies with own people, own branches and own systems and they happen to sell financial services.
PIERRE DE VOS Here the company is sitting in a position because of unlawful contract They have all this information about more than 10 million people. And according to allegations they use this information to make a profit. That information is not their information it is the state information. overlap between state and private company. Huge ethical problems.

CPS’s legal representative argued in court that if the CPS contract was going to be extended, they would need a market-related increase.
SERGE BELAMANT We are a public company you know, I have shareholders. If I don't’ do it for something profitable my shareholders will say can we get a new CEO that works in interest of company.
But the court ordered that the extention of CPS’s contract was made on the same terms and conditions than the existing contract.
The Concourt also ordered that Sassa needed to appoint independent legal practitioners and technical experts who will monitor the implementation of grants, and to evaluate steps taken by Sassa in a bidding process or if Sassa intended to take over the payment process.
Professor de Vos says the court indicated a vote of no-confidence in Minister Dlamini and Sassa, with the following order:
JUSTICE FRONEMAN File reports on affidavit with this Court every three months, setting out the steps they have taken to evaluate the matter, the result of the matter and any further steps to be taken.
By the end of March, Minister Dlamini needs to hand in an affadavit to the court to show cause why she shouldn’t pay the costs of this application from her own pocket.
PROMOS PROMO 1: 15”

DLAMINI: There is no crisis…

The Minister of Social Development’s view was not echoed by the Chief Justice of South Africa. Carte Blanche unpacks the Sassa saga.

PROMO 2: 15”

SERGE BELAMANT: We don’t have or need the database. Peole have impression that The SASSA database is worth his weight in gold.

With no Plan B from Sassa or the Department of Social Development, the Constitutional Court once again had to save the day.

Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 19 March 2017 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 29 March 2017 Press Release: SASSA In April 2014 the Constitutional Court ruled that the contract with Cash Paymaster Services for paying out social grants to beneficiaries was invalid and ordered the Department of Social Development and the SA Social Security Agency (SASSA) to find a solution. With two weeks left to go before CPS's current contract expires, and grants to 17 million beneficiaries at stake, Carte Blanche asks: Why did the Department of Social Development and SASSA wait three years to find a new service provider? Script: SASSA FACING THE MUSIC SCRIPT PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK PRESENTER: BONGANI BINGWA EDITOR: STENETTE GROSSKOPF BROADCAST DATE: 19 MARCH 2017 JUSTICE FRONEMAN: The sole reason for the litigation leading to this judgment, is the failure of Sassa and the Minister to keep their promise to this court and the people of South Africa. Our constitution provides that everyone has the right to have access to social security – which includes government’s payment of social grants to 17 million beneficiaries. On Friday, the Constitutional Court ruled that Social Development Minister, Bathabile Dlamini and the South African Social Security Agency broke their promises to secure the pay-out of these grants from the 1st of April -after the existing contract with private service provider, Cash Paymasters Services, expires. This left the Concourt no choice but to extend CPS’s contract, ruled Justice Johan Froneman, who the wrote the judgment. JUSTICE FRONEMAN: The underlying danger to us all is that when the institutions of government established under the Constitution are undermined, the fabric of our society comes under threat. Our order reflects that Sassa and CPS should continue to fulfill its respective obligations of the payment of social grants for a period of 12 months as an extention of the current contract. Once again, the Constitutional Court saved the day. EMILY MAZIBUKO & VIRGINIA NKOSI VIRGINIA: And the government must do something because we depending to the government. EMILY: Too much VIRGINIA: We can’t do anything, we dpm’t wrok EMILY: Got no money VIRGINIA: Got no money EMILY: Got nothing BONGANI LINK The vast majority of grant recipients of grants are children and the elderly. For women like Emily Mazibuko and Virginia Nkosi this is a life-line. Without the grant, millions of people will be left destitute. Despite the anxiety felt on the ground, President Jacob Zuma and Minister Dlamini repeatedly stated there was no “crisis”. MINISTER BATHABILE DLAMINI All eligible social grants beneficiries will receive their money on 1st April and beyond. There is no crisis at Sassa. A view not echoed by Chief Justice Mogoeng Mogoeng during the arguments heard on Wednesday in the case brought by NGO Black Sash asking the court to take oversight of a new contract to ensure the payments of social grants. JUSTICE MOGOENG MOGOENG This is a crisis. We must do whatever is necessary to intervene to avoid the proliferation of the crisis. Sassa awarded the contract to CPS in 2012. However, in 2013, the Constitutional Court declared the contract invalid due to a flawed Sassa tender process, but also suspended the invalidity to guarantee the payments of the grants. The court instructed Sassa to reissue the tender. In 2015, Sassa informed the Concourt that no suitable bidder was found and detailed how it planned to take over the payments of the grants itself. Due to Sassa’s compliance, the Concourt relinquished its supervisory jurisdiction. And this is when the shenanigans started, says Constitutional law expert Professor Pierre de Vos. PIERRE DE VOS Treasury says this is a self created crisis and it is difficult to disagree with Treasury. Prof de Vos says he’s not surprised that the Concourt gave such stringent orders given the history of the case. PIERRE DE VOS But when they discovered they will not be able to fix the matter they didn't’ go back to the court, and they didn’t make alternative plans and there is no plan B. JUSTICE FRONEMAN Since April 2016 the responsible functionaries of SASSA have been aware that it could not comply with the undertaking to the Court that it would be able to pay social grants from 1 April this year. The Minister was apparently informed of this only in October 2016. ADV GEOFF BUDLENDER/BLACK SASH: The payment of social grants is the Minister’s most important responsibility. She claims that she was kept in the dark for six months about the fact that sassa would not be able to pay the grants. With due respect, that’s simply incomprehensible BONGANI LINK: It is now widely accepted that this crisis could and should have been avoided. And so at the centre at the arguments that are being presented here, is that it must never happen again. And that regardless of whatever contract is signed, the court must exercise its jurisdiction over the implementation. CHIEF JUSTICE MOGOENG MOGOENG: How do we get to this level of what could be mistakenbly or aguably be charachterised as absolute incompetence? How? ADV ANDREW BREITENBACH/SASSA & MINISTER DLAMINI The business of social grants to 17 million people, if you’re looking at card holders and beneficiaries is fanatstically complex. It involved a multitude of stakeholders, a very great expertise, and yes, very large sums of money that I’vementioned has been paid out to CPS. In spite of all the jubilation from involved parties, who really won the day? During the past few weeks, opposition parties increasingly called for Minister Dlamini’s head – more so after the Concourt pointed to her apparent incompetence. LIEZEL VAN DER MERWE/IFP MP Finally, honourable Minister, you have broken your oath of office, you’re in contempt of court, you’ve trampelled on our Constitution, you’ve shown disdain for those most vulnerable in our sociaty, It’s time to go! Yet, there is no indication that action will be taken against Minister Dlamini. In fact, in his first Q&A session in Parliament on Thursday, President Jacob Zuma defended her vigorously – even though he has fired ministers for much less in the past. PRESIDENT JACOB ZUMA: I thought the date that we that are talking about has not arrived: the 1st of April. Now, this is another kind of democracy that if you suspect that somebody is going to fail, or make a mistake, you must punish that person before it happens. PIERRE DE VOS The President is person with whom buck stops. He is the head of cabinet and executive. He is ultimately responsible for the department. And not only does her job seem secure in spite of this, but the Minister also got what she seemingly wanted – to keep CPS as the sole service provider. JUSTICE FRONEMAN The Minister and Sassa assured us that CPS is the only provider that can do this PIERRE DE VOS In context of existing agreement with a company who got a contract to deliver the grants, based on an unlawful and invalid tender. So suspicions will arise that for reason either SASSA or minister is protecting the private company and the profits. Advocate Norman Arendse SC – who was the chairperson of the National Adjudication Committee in 2007/08 who also oversaw the first national Sassa tender, says the Sassa/CPS contract is one of the biggest government tenders. ADV NORMAN ARENDSE ADV ARENDSE: It is a project bigger than arms deal. I am afraid that big projects in SA and all over world will often become subject of corrupt activities. that is why it is important to ensure that is must be evaluated and adjudicated by people of integrity. BONGANI What do you mean it is bigger than the arms deal? ADV NORMAN ARENDSE ADV ARENDSE: the payments itself it exceeds R130 billion a year. IF you are getting a contract over five years it does exceed the arms deal. Already nine years ago during the 2007/8 bidding process, the National adjudication Committee recommended that beneficiaries’ personal data was to be protected and that the sell-on of it to third parties to be prohibited. Yet, the same point of contention was one of the most critical factors in Black Sash’s Concourt application and the court again made it an order. JUSTICE FRONEMAN Precludes a contracting party from inviting beneficiaries to “opt-in” to the sharing of confidential information for the marketing of goods and services. By its own admission, subsidiary companies of Net1 – the CPS umbrella company that’s listed on the JSE and Nasdaq – sells insurance, electricity, airtime and is also a microlender. But CPS CEO, Serge Belamant denies that they are selling on beneficiaries’ personal data. SERGE BELAMANT We don’t have or need the database. Peole have impression that The SASSA database is worth his weight in gold. It has an ID number and name. BONGANI So ultimately, without that data base, how would you sell your products? SERGE BELAMANT The way we do it now. We would have 150 brances, we would put up posters, we would be doing advertising, people would come to our branches and buy the product, like they buy it from anyone else. Magda Wierzycka, who owns her own JSE-listed financial services group, says Net1 makes huge profits from selling these services to grant beneficiaries. MAGDA WIERZYCKA Grant recipients amount of a revenue of 2.6 billion rand over one year and profit of over 790 million. BONGANI THAT MEANS THEY MAKE MORE FROM FINANCIAL SERVICES … THAN ANY OTHER ASPECT OF CONTRACT. MAGDA WIERZYCKA 100% so it really is about microloans and life insurance. So they make a profit per annum of grant recipients of roughly 6.7 billion rand and profit of 1.5 billion rand. BONGANI ISNT’ YOUR BUSINESS MODEL THAT YOU MAKE MORE FROM SERVICING THE BENEFICIARIES OF THE SASSA CONTRACT THAN YOU DO FROM DISPENSING THE GRNATS. SERGE BELAMANT Is there a problem with that??? What is the problem with that? BONGANI SO WHEN YOU SAY .. THAT VERY FEW OF EMPOLOYEES ARE ONES SELLIGN THESE PRODUCTS THOSE STATEMENTS ARE AT ODDS WITH EACH OTHER. SERGE BELAMANT Why would you say that. On one hand you have CPS it is ring fenced they are only focused on dispersement on grants. then multiple companies with own people, own branches and own systems and they happen to sell financial services. PIERRE DE VOS Here the company is sitting in a position because of unlawful contract They have all this information about more than 10 million people. And according to allegations they use this information to make a profit. That information is not their information it is the state information. overlap between state and private company. Huge ethical problems. CPS’s legal representative argued in court that if the CPS contract was going to be extended, they would need a market-related increase. SERGE BELAMANT We are a public company you know, I have shareholders. If I don't’ do it for something profitable my shareholders will say can we get a new CEO that works in interest of company. But the court ordered that the extention of CPS’s contract was made on the same terms and conditions than the existing contract. The Concourt also ordered that Sassa needed to appoint independent legal practitioners and technical experts who will monitor the implementation of grants, and to evaluate steps taken by Sassa in a bidding process or if Sassa intended to take over the payment process. Professor de Vos says the court indicated a vote of no-confidence in Minister Dlamini and Sassa, with the following order: JUSTICE FRONEMAN File reports on affidavit with this Court every three months, setting out the steps they have taken to evaluate the matter, the result of the matter and any further steps to be taken. By the end of March, Minister Dlamini needs to hand in an affadavit to the court to show cause why she shouldn’t pay the costs of this application from her own pocket. PROMOS PROMO 1: 15” DLAMINI: There is no crisis… The Minister of Social Development’s view was not echoed by the Chief Justice of South Africa. Carte Blanche unpacks the Sassa saga. PROMO 2: 15” SERGE BELAMANT: We don’t have or need the database. Peole have impression that The SASSA database is worth his weight in gold. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Come April, 1st, will the 17-million people receiving social grants from government be receiving their money. Social Development Minister Dlamini is adamant they will, but chances look dim.
metadata.Further information: The fiasco over who will pay social grants and how they will be paid is far from over, prompting a last-minute crisis meeting yesterday between President Jacob Zuma, Social Development Minister Bathabile Dlamini and Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan. And now the crisis that threatens the livelihoods of more than 17 million South Africans is pitting Dlamini against Treasury and her Cabinet colleagues. City Press understands that although the department of social development reached an agreement to secure a contract to distribute grants with Cash Paymaster Services (CPS) late Friday night, this still needs to be approved by Treasury, which is not in favour of it. Treasury officials insist the deal can only be condoned if it is within the law and the allocated budget. Dlamini’s handling of the crisis has also pitted her against her own senior officials, who have refused to follow her orders. Some have alleged this was a manufactured crisis and the strategy all along was to ensure that CPS continued to hold the contract. They have also accused Dlamini of deliberately blocking all attempts to resolve the impasse. One senior government official told City Press: “It was clear to me that processes to find a solution were being deliberately delayed so that the contract could go to CPS. They were even ignoring advice from senior advocate Wim Trengove, who was suggesting possible solutions.” Treasury seems to agree that the crisis was self-made. In a letter last month, Solly Tshitangano, Treasury’s chief director of supply chain management governance, monitoring and compliance, wrote: “The SA Social Security Agency (Sassa) should have requested a deviation to advertise a new tender for a short period from December 2016 to early January 2017 to avoid a self-created emergency.” Lumka Oliphant, Dlamini’s spokesperson, did not respond to requests for comment this week. Asked to respond to allegations that the grants crisis was created deliberately to benefit CPS, Sassa spokesperson Kgomoco Diseko said: “These remain claims and not fact. "We put this contract out in the market in a transparent manner and the market failed us.” In 2014, the Constitutional Court ruled that the process Sassa had followed to award the contract to CPS was extremely flawed and had to be scrapped. The state was given three years to correct it or find a new service provider. The deadline to do so is March 31. Sassa has not awarded a new tender and with just less than four weeks to go, it remains unclear how the grants to South Africa’s poorest are going to be paid. No end in sight After weeks of panic, the social development department announced in a short statement on Friday that the nature of the agreement it had reached with CPS would be communicated “in due course”. No details were revealed. But government officials say whatever agreement was reached, it would still need to be condoned by Treasury. But Treasury has long made it clear that it would not support the extension of a contract declared invalid by the Constitutional Court. A government official privy to developments warned: “If Treasury condones something this big, knowing that it could have been prevented and that the urgent situation was deliberately created, then you are weakening the fiscus rules of procurement.” Last month, Treasury turned down Sassa’s request to be allowed to deviate from the Public Finance Management Act and approve the extension of CPS’s existing contract. It also wanted to hike the company’s initially agreed rate of R16.44 per beneficiary to between R22 and R25 per payee. Turning down the request, Tshitangano wrote: “Requesting National Treasury to extend a contract that was declared invalid by the highest court will not only be seen as being defiant to the judicial system, but may further be seen as perpetuating the illegal and unconstitutional deviation actions reprimanded by the highest court in the land.” Political ammunition However, officials are concerned that if Treasury refuses to condone the agreement with CPS, that could be used as further ammunition to discredit it and portray it as uncaring towards the country’s poor. Gordhan has come under attack from various Zuma supporters, who have accused him of driving an anti-poor budget. In a statement after yesterday’s meeting, the presidency said Zuma “is of the view that the matters are solvable”. “He has directed the two ministers [Dlamini and Gordhan] to mandate their technical teams to work on the outstanding issues in order to ensure that social grant beneficiaries receive their grants on April 1.” City Press has learnt that Treasury was expected to be pressured at the meeting to “assist” social development. But Treasury has said it would only regularise an agreement with CPS if the Constitutional Court extended the suspension of the invalid contract. However, even if Treasury was pushed to sign off on the agreement, there was still no guarantee that the Constitutional Court would endorse it. Sassa and Dlamini are due to appear before the Constitutional Court on March 15 to defend government in an application brought against them by civil rights organisation Black Sash. Treasury has warned that even if the department of social development said it no longer wanted an extension while implementing a new contract, this would still be unlawful. This is because any new contract is required to go through an open, competitive and fair tender process. If not, other parties would be able to challenge the contract in court because they were not allowed an opportunity to bid. The shambles Dlamini created Dlamini has been slammed for her handling of the crisis, particularly for her reluctance to allow officials to report to the Constitutional Court. On February 28, Sassa filed papers in that court, asking it to authorise negotiations with CPS with a view to entering into another contract. But the agency later withdrew those papers, allegedly on Dlamini’s orders. This led to a fallout with the department of social development’s new director-general, Zane Dangor, who had only been in the position for three months. Dangor resigned on Friday. He confirmed his resignation on Saturday, saying it was prompted by a breakdown in the relationship between him and Dlamini, and a deep disagreement about how the crisis was being managed. “This [dispute] was particularly [about] issues related to Sassa’s legal obligations in relation to the Constitutional Court,” he said. Parliament’s standing committee on public accounts (Scopa) issued a statement yesterday, saying it noted his resignation with anger. “In our brief interactions with Mr Dangor, he had proven himself to be an honest and hard-working civil servant. "He was one of the many officials in the department of social development and in Sassa who have been frustrated by Minister Bathabile Dlamini’s heavy-handed interference in Sassa’s administrative matters.” Scopa has scheduled a meeting with Dlamini on Tuesday. Senior social development officials told City Press that Dlamini sidelined Sassa chief executive Thokozani Magwaza and other officials, preferring to work directly with Zodwa Mvulane, appointed as special programme leader on new payment systems. Sassa and Dlamini claim in court papers, filed on Friday in response to the legal challenge by Black Sash, that they made it clear from the start that a complete takeover by government of social grant payments was dependent on the outcome of “various consultations”. They say this was flagged in November 2015 in a report handed to the Constitutional Court, which had taken on a supervisory role. The department initially promised to develop the capacity to pay the grants itself, but Dlamini and Sassa say in their legal papers that they were advised by a technical team that the plan was “overly optimistic, unrealistic and underpinned by insufficient research”. The reason for this was that Sassa did not have the budget, internal capacity and enough skilled people to implement the plan. Dlamini went on to claim in court papers this week that she only became aware of the scale of the problem in October. “As at late August or early September 2016, Sassa officials started to fully appreciate that Sassa will not be in a position to substantially implement the progress report within the time frames specified. "The minister appreciated the position in October. The minister and Sassa accept that they ought to have been aware earlier,” they say in court papers. The technical team, they claimed, advised Sassa to continue to use CPS beyond the March deadline for at least the next two to three years. This contradicted legal advice from Trengove that the proposed interim agreement with CPS would not be legal. Trengove found there would be nothing left to renew with CPS.
